steps.explanationAfterStep: The OH group is now OH₂⁺: it can leave as a neutral water molecule, a good leaving group.
A secondary carbocation: not very stable. Its neighbour carries a C–H bond on a carbon with two methyl groups, which matters next.
Also correct: the hydride can shift as water leaves, so the poor secondary cation never fully forms. Both pictures appear in textbooks.
The hydrogen moves with its bonding pair (as a hydride), so the positive charge ends up on the carbon it left. That carbon is tertiary: three alkyl groups stabilise it.
2-Bromo-2-methylbutane: the bromine ends up on a different carbon from the one that carried the OH, the signature of a carbocation rearrangement.

title: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol and HBr
subtitle: A hydride shift moves the bromine
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 15
Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 36

reactants.caption: 3-methylbutan-2-ol + HBr
hintTiers: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group. How can the OH group be made into a better one?
The oxygen of the alcohol takes the proton of HBr; the H–Br pair goes onto bromine. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair on the alcohol oxygen forms a bond to the hydrogen of HBr. Arrow 2: the H–Br bond breaks, and its pair goes onto bromine.
reactants.learnerPrompt: HBr is a strong acid. Show the first step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide is a strong base and a very poor leaving group. Protonate the oxygen first, so that water leaves instead.
Bromide cannot push out hydroxide, a very poor leaving group. The acid must protonate the oxygen first.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the oxygen takes the proton. Hydrogen can only have one bond, so what happens to the H–Br bond?

oxonium-ion.caption: protonated alcohol + bromide
hintTiers: The C–O bond breaks, and water leaves with both electrons. What kind of carbon is left with the charge?
The C–O bond breaks heterolytically, its pair going onto oxygen. One arrow, leaving a secondary carbocation.
The C–O bond breaks, and its pair goes onto the oxygen, which leaves as water.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: SN2 at this secondary carbon, next to a branch point, is slow. The product is rearranged, which shows that a carbocation forms.
The C–O pair goes to the oxygen, which leaves as neutral water.

tertiary-cation.caption: tertiary carbocation after the hydride shift
hintTiers: Which species has lone pairs and a negative charge? Which carbon is now positive?
A bromide lone pair forms a bond to the tertiary positive carbon. One arrow.
A lone pair on bromide forms a new bond to the tertiary positive carbon.
tertiary-cation.learnerPrompt: Bromide captures the cation. Draw the final step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: After the shift, the carbon that lost water has four bonds and no charge. The positive charge is now on the tertiary carbon.
Water could add, but in concentrated HBr the tertiary alcohol formed would simply lose water again. Bromide traps the cation for good.

secondary-cation.caption: secondary carbocation + water + bromide
hintTiers: A tertiary carbocation is more stable than a secondary one. Which neighbouring bond could move to put the charge on a tertiary carbon?
The C–H bond on the neighbouring carbon moves, with its hydrogen, onto the positive carbon: a 1,2-hydride shift. One arrow.
The C–H bond of the neighbouring carbon becomes a new C–H bond to the positive carbon (point at the dashed line).
secondary-cation.learnerPrompt: Before bromide arrives, the cation rearranges. Draw the shift.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Bromide could trap this secondary cation, and a little 2-bromo-3-methylbutane does form. But the hydride shift to a tertiary cation is faster, so the main product is rearranged.
A methyl shift would give another secondary cation: nothing gained. Move the hydrogen, which leaves a tertiary cation.

mechanismSummary: Protonation turns OH into a good leaving group. Water leaves to give a secondary carbocation, which rearranges by a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable tertiary cation before bromide adds. A rearranged product is evidence for a carbocation, and so for SN1.
